# Network lab 6: Lock down the switch (Network Simulator)

Shut unused ports, allow one known device per staff port with port security, protect the console and enable modes, and watch an unknown laptop get blocked.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `netbuilder.json`, `README.txt`.

## 1. Park and shut the unused ports

A live, empty wall port is an open door: anyone can plug in. Double-click **sw1** for its CLI:

```
enable
configure terminal
vlan 999
 name PARKING
interface range fa0/21 - 24
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 999
 shutdown
end
show interfaces status
```

- [ ] VLAN 999 made
- [ ] Ports 21-24 in VLAN 999 and shut down
- [ ] show interfaces status shows them disabled

> Hint: Shut ports show as "disabled" in `show interfaces status`.

?> Which command switches a port off? :: sha256:08434ba9cdf55a02284e2913400586cd289878e0f055f7bb0b07ce392caeb989

## 2. One known device per staff port

```
configure terminal
interface range fa0/1 - 12
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 1
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security violation shutdown
end
```

From staff-1's Command Prompt, ping staff-2 (192.168.10.12), so both staff ports hear from their computers, then run `show port-security` on the switch. (On a real switch, a port that has never heard from its computer learns whatever plugs in first.)

- [ ] Port security on ports 1-12
- [ ] Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 each show 1 current address
- [ ] show port-security checked

> Hint: Sticky learns the first MAC address seen on the port and keeps it in the configuration.

?> How many MAC addresses may each staff port learn? :: sha256:6b86b273ff34fce19d6b804eff5a3f5747ada4eaa22f1d49c01e52ddb7875b4b

## 3. Plug in an unknown laptop

Click the cable between staff-2 and the switch and press **Unplug it**. Add a **Laptop** from the bar, give it 192.168.10.50 in its panel, and cable it to **Fa0/2** with **Copper Straight-Through**. Ping staff-1 from the laptop. Look at the link light, then run `show interfaces status` and `show port-security` on the switch.

The port has shut itself down. To bring it back after a check, unplug the laptop, plug staff-2 back into Fa0/2, and on that port run `shutdown` then `no shutdown` (on a real switch the port stays err-disabled until you do).

- [ ] Unknown laptop blocked
- [ ] Port state read in show interfaces status
- [ ] staff-2 back on Fa0/2 and connected

> Hint: The link light turns red and the status says err-disabled.

?> Which status does show interfaces status give the blocked port? :: sha256:1362b4e68ac510d9a8b75001b1e8d919e8786718159c86b2aa49b8dcf852ebf8

## 4. Protect the management access

Anyone with a console cable could change all of this. Add passwords:

```
configure terminal
enable secret <choose one>
line console 0
 password <choose another>
 login
end
copy running-config startup-config
show running-config
```

Read the top of `show running-config`: the enable secret is stored as a hash (`enable secret 5 ...`), never as the word you typed.

- [ ] enable secret set
- [ ] Console password with login
- [ ] Configuration saved ([OK])

> Hint: `enable secret` is stored as a hash; the old `enable password` isn't. Always use secret.

?> Which command saves the configuration so it survives a restart? :: sha256:a1783b4880d1183614ecc1ec240ae65317cc72d4c2dfc8c9251d2a1986a3ac6c

## 5. Where next

Unused ports shut, known devices only, management protected. Lab 7 adds the access list that keeps guests away from staff.

script.intro: Welcome to network lab six. Think of Tulsi Travels' switch as a building. Right now every door is unlocked, even in the empty rooms, and the key to the building manager's office hangs on the front door. Today we fix that with the short checklist network teams run on every new switch: shut the unused ports, allow one known device per staff desk, and lock the management access. Then we try to get in with an unknown laptop. Lab five's network is already built for you.
script.outro: Hardening isn't clever. It's a short checklist done every time: shut what you don't use, allow only what you know, lock the management, save the configuration. When one of those steps is skipped, an intruder rarely needs anything clever either. See you in lab seven.

steps.say: Step one: park and shut the unused ports. Double-click the switch for its CLI. Create VLAN 999 and name it PARKING. Then take ports 21 to 24, make them access ports in VLAN 999, and shut them down. End, then show interfaces status.
steps.after: Ports 21 to 24 now show as disabled, in VLAN 999. Why both, the parking VLAN and the shutdown? A live wall port in an empty office is an open door: anyone can plug in a laptop and they're on the network. Shutting the port closes the door. Parking it in a VLAN that leads nowhere means that if someone turns it back on by mistake, it still connects to nothing. Two locks, because one of them will fail one day. The command that switches a port off is shutdown.

steps.say: Step two: one known device per staff port. On ports 1 to 12, turn on port security, set the maximum to one MAC address, make it sticky, and set the violation action to shutdown. Then, from staff-1's Command Prompt, ping staff-2 at 192.168.10.12, so both ports hear from their computers. Finally, run show port-security on the switch.
steps.after: show port-security lists Fa0/1 to Fa0/12, each with a maximum of one secure address and the action Shutdown. Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 show one current address each: staff-1 and staff-2. Sticky means the switch keeps the first MAC address it saw on the port and writes it into the running configuration, so it stays. That's why the ping matters on a real switch: a port that has never heard from its computer would simply learn whoever plugs in first. From now on each staff port accepts its own computer and nothing else. Each staff port may learn one MAC address.

steps.say: Step three: plug in an unknown laptop. Click the cable between staff-2 and the switch and press Unplug it. Add a laptop from the bar, give it 192.168.10.50, and cable it to Fa0/2 with Copper Straight-Through. Ping staff-1 from the laptop, and watch the link light. Then, on the switch, run show interfaces status and show port-security.
steps.after: The ping fails, and the light on Fa0/2 turns red. show interfaces status says err-disabled. show port-security shows a security violation count of one on Fa0/2. The switch saw an unknown device on a port that allows one known one, and shut the port, exactly as we told it to. In real life, that's someone unplugging the office PC to plug in their own machine, and the network saying no. To bring the port back once you've checked who it was, unplug the laptop, plug staff-2 back in, then on interface fa0/2 type shutdown, and then no shutdown. On a real switch, the port stays err-disabled until you do. The blocked port's status is err-disabled.

steps.say: Step four: protect the management access. Anyone with a console cable could undo everything we just did. So in configuration mode, set an enable secret. Then go to line console 0, set a password, and type login, so the password is actually asked for. End, save with copy running-config startup-config, and then look at show running-config.
steps.after: The save prints Building configuration, then OK. At the top of the running configuration you'll see enable secret 5, followed by a scrambled string, not the word you typed. Two details matter. Use enable secret, never the older enable password: the secret is stored as a one-way hash, while enable password sits in the configuration in plain text, or behind a weak scramble that's easy to reverse. And save. The running configuration lives in memory; if the switch restarts before you copy it to the startup configuration, today's work is gone. The save command is copy running-config startup-config. Choose your own passwords, and write them in your notes, not in the lab files.

steps.say: That's lab six: unused ports shut and parked, one known device per desk, and management locked and saved. Lab seven adds the access list that keeps guests away from staff.
